claim: An LLM evaluation framework is distinct from an academic benchmark, an evaluation platform, an observability platform, and a guardrail -- its primary job is to tell you whether a version of your LLM application is better than another before you ship it.
stance_target: terminology/taxonomy for eval tooling selection in an agentic software factory
quoted_support: the primary job of an evaluation framework is to tell you whether a version of your LLM application is better than another before you ship it.

claim: AI-agent tracing -- tracing a failed evaluation score back to the specific tool call, retriever step, LLM call, or sub-agent that caused it -- is a key differentiator among LLM eval frameworks, with Promptfoo explicitly lacking native component-level agent-tracing support.
stance_target: observability-grade granularity needed for debugging multi-agent pipeline failures
scope_conditions: comparison of DeepEval, Promptfoo, Ragas, Arize Phoenix, TruLens as of 2026
quoted_support: AI agent tracing: can a failed score be traced back to the tool, retriever, LLM call, or AI sub-agent that caused it? ... Promptfoo: Not supported: no native component-level scoring

claim: A developer-workflow criterion for choosing an eval framework is whether AI coding agents (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex) can themselves use it as an evaluation harness to run tests, inspect failures, and verify fixes.
stance_target: agent-usable eval tooling as infrastructure for self-correcting agentic development loops
quoted_support: Can AI coding agents such as Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex use it as an evaluation harness to run tests, inspect failures, make targeted changes, and verify the result?
